Looking at this problem, I need to determine whether the local fractional seminorm at a point vanishes as the radius shrinks, given that the global fractional seminorm is finite.

**Answer: Yes, it is true.**

**Proof.**

By the change of variables $h = y - x$ (so $y = x+h$, $dy = dh$, $|x-y| = |h|$) and Tonelli's theorem (the integrand is non-negative), the finiteness assumption gives:

$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|^p}{|x-y|^{n+\alpha p}}\,dx\,dy = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\frac{|f(x+h)-f(x)|^p}{|h|^{n+\alpha p}}\,dh\right)dx < \infty.$$

Define
$$G(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\frac{|f(x+h)-f(x)|^p}{|h|^{n+\alpha p}}\,dh.$$

Since the double integral is finite, $G \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and consequently $G(x) < \infty$ for almost every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

Now fix any $x$ with $G(x) < \infty$. Define the non-negative measurable function
$$\psi_x(h) := \frac{|f(x+h)-f(x)|^p}{|h|^{n+\alpha p}}, \qquad h \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}.$$

The finiteness $G(x) < \infty$ means exactly that $\psi_x \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

For $r > 0$, set
$$G_r(x) := \int_{B(0,r)} \psi_x(h)\,dh = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \mathbf{1}_{B(0,r)}(h)\,\psi_x(h)\,dh.$$

As $r \to 0$, the indicator $\mathbf{1}_{B(0,r)}(h) \to 0$ for every $h \neq 0$, i.e., for almost every $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Moreover, $\mathbf{1}_{B(0,r)}(h)\,\psi_x(h) \leq \psi_x(h) \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$. By the **Dominated Convergence Theorem**,

$$G_r(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \mathbf{1}_{B(0,r)}(h)\,\psi_x(h)\,dh \;\longrightarrow\; 0 \quad \text{as } r \to 0.$$

This holds for every $x$ with $G(x) < \infty$, which is a set of full measure. Therefore,

$$\int_{B(0,r)}\frac{|f(x+h)-f(x)|^p}{|h|^{n+\alpha p}}\,dh \to 0 \quad \text{as } r \to 0$$

for almost every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. $\blacksquare$
